lesson.title: Lists: Python's All-Purpose Container
lesson.summary: An introduction to the list, Python's ordered, mutable collection type that can hold any combination of values.
lesson.body:
Every variable you have used so far has held exactly one value: one number, one string, one boolean. Real programs rarely work that way. A gradebook needs to hold every quiz score for a student, a to-do app needs to hold every task, and a game needs to hold every item in a player's inventory. For that, Python gives you the list, a single variable that holds an ordered sequence of values, one after another, in the order you put them in.

A list is written with square brackets, with the individual values, called elements, separated by commas. Because a list is itself one of Python's data types, sitting alongside int, float, str, and bool, you can store a list in a variable just like any other value, and you can also store any of those other data types inside a list.

scores = [88, 92, 79, 95]
print(scores)
print(type(scores))
print(len(scores))

Running this prints [88, 92, 79, 95] on the first line, because that is simply how Python displays a list back to you. The second line prints <class 'list'>, confirming that scores really is a list object and not, say, a string that merely looks like one. The third line prints 4, because len() counts the elements, and there are four scores in the list.

A list does not require every element to be the same type. You could just as easily write mixed = ["Amir", 16, True, 3.9], and Python would accept it without complaint, holding a string, an integer, a boolean, and a float side by side in one container. In practice, most lists you write will be homogeneous, meaning every element is the same type, because that makes the list easier to reason about and process with a loop, but Python itself never enforces that convention.

What makes lists especially powerful is that they are ordered and they remember position. The first element you write is always at the front, the second is always right after it, and so on, which means you can ask a list "what is your third item" and get a reliable answer every time. That ordering is what makes indexing and slicing possible, and it is also what makes a for loop over a list predictable: it visits elements in exactly the order they were stored, not some scrambled order.

Lists also share something important with your earlier work on loop patterns: a list is frequently the thing a loop iterates over. Where you once wrote for i in range(5) to repeat an action five times, you will now often write for score in scores to do something with each individual score, letting the list itself define both how many times the loop runs and what value is available on each pass. That shift, from looping over a count to looping over real data, is one of the most important habits this concept sets up, and every list concept that follows, creating them, indexing into them, slicing them, and modifying them, builds directly on the idea introduced here: a list is an ordered container that remembers exactly what you put in it and exactly where you put it.
